input: The staffing question for the maintenance crew is, at bottom, a question about the shape of the year rather than about the size of the crew in the abstract. The crew currently numbers 16 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 7% of paid hours last year. One way of softening that overtime is to replace half of it with one additional hire, and the cost of doing so is $63k per year fully loaded. Set against that cost is an awkward pattern in the overtime itself: it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, which means the hours the new hire would replace are not spread evenly across the calendar. A hire, however, is paid for the full year, in the quiet months just as in the peak months. The trade-off is therefore built into the structure of the case: the benefit of the hire arrives in the peak periods, where the cover is needed, while the cost of the hire runs continuously through the periods where it is not. Any judgement on the proposal has to weigh a full-year cost against a peak-season benefit, and the figures as stated offer no way around that weighing. Seen in that light, the proposal is neither plainly cheap nor plainly dear; it is a proposal whose cost and whose benefit arrive on different calendars, and it stands or falls on how much the peak cover is worth to the operation that has to staff those peaks.
target: The maintenance crew has 16 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 7% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $63k per year fully loaded. The trade-off is in the pattern of the overtime: the overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and a hire is paid for the full year. The hire's cost therefore runs through the quiet periods at the same rate as through the peaks, while the overtime it replaces falls only in the peaks. The case for the hire rests on cover in the peak periods; the case against rests on a cost that does not follow the pattern of the work. No figure for the cost of the overtime being replaced is stated, and the comparison is carried on the hire's cost and the overtime share alone. At the stated figures, the decision turns on whether peak cover is worth a full-year cost at the stated rate. Fully loaded cost is the whole cost of the hire: the wage and every employment cost that travels with it, stated for the full year. The overtime share is stated for the year that has passed, and the pattern within that year is the part of the evidence that decides the case. Peaks concentrate the overtime into short periods, and cover bought for a peak is cover that must be present in that period and is paid for outside it. The crew size enters the case only as the base the overtime share is measured against; the share itself, and the cost of replacing half of it, are the operative figures.
